items.title: Water has the highest specific heat of any common liquid
items.claim: It takes 4.18 J to warm 1 g of water by 1°C. The same amount of energy raises 1 g of iron by 9.3°C, 1 g of copper by 11°C, 1 g of mercury by 30°C. Water is exceptionally hard to warm — and to cool.
items.prompt: Why is water's heat capacity so high?

options.text: Heat energy in water is shared between molecular vibrations, rotations, and the breaking and re-forming of hydrogen bonds; the hydrogen-bonding 'sink' absorbs huge amounts of energy with only modest temperature rise
Water is denser than most liquids

items.reveal:
When you heat water, energy doesn't just speed molecules up. A significant fraction goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds. These bonds are about 23 kJ/mol — much smaller than O-H covalent bonds (463 kJ/mol) but much larger than typical thermal energy.

This is why coastal climates are mild: oceans absorb and release heat slowly. The Gulf Stream warms northwest Europe by carrying tropical heat north. Water's heat capacity buffers the climate.

It's also why sweating cools you so effectively: evaporating 1 g of water absorbs 2260 J (latent heat of vaporisation) — far more than the same mass of any common solvent.
items.why: Specific heat is taught as a number to look up. It is a measure of how many ways a substance can absorb energy at the molecular level.

items.title: Frost forms by water vapour skipping the liquid state entirely
items.claim: Water vapour in cold air can deposit directly onto a windowpane as ice crystals without ever becoming liquid. The reverse — solid to gas without melting — is called sublimation, and is how freeze-drying works.
items.prompt: Why does water sometimes skip the liquid stage?

options.text: Water bends the laws of phase transitions
At pressures below the triple point (6.1 mbar for water) the liquid phase is not stable — water can only exist as solid or vapour, and transitions go directly between them
Frost forms only from existing ice
Liquid water is too dense for cold air

items.reveal_title: Below the triple point, liquid disappears
items.reveal:
Water's triple point sits at 0.01°C and 6.1 millibar — the only temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist. Below this pressure the liquid phase is unstable; water can only be vapour or ice, and crossing the boundary means sublimation or deposition.

At atmospheric pressure (1013 mbar) water can be liquid between 0 and 100°C, but small pockets of supercooled vapour near a cold surface can deposit straight to solid because the local equilibrium prefers ice over the metastable liquid intermediate.

Freeze-drying exploits this: freeze food, lower the pressure below the triple point, and the ice sublimes away with no melting. The structure is preserved, water is removed, and the result is light, stable food (instant coffee, astronaut meals, pharmaceutical formulations).
items.why: Solid to gas skipping liquid is treated as a curiosity. It is the dominant transition at low pressure and underpins multibillion-dollar industries.

items.title: The modern atomic theory began with a colour-blind Quaker schoolmaster
items.claim: In 1803-1808 John Dalton, a Quaker schoolteacher in Manchester with no university post, proposed that elements are made of indivisible atoms with fixed mass. Compounds form by simple integer ratios of atoms. His theory still underpins everything in chemistry.
items.prompt: What evidence convinced chemists Dalton was right?

options.text: He saw atoms with a microscope

The law of multiple proportions: when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios (e.g. carbon to oxygen is 1:1.33 in CO and 1:2.67 in CO2)

items.reveal_title: Whole-number ratios point to discrete particles
items.reveal:
Dalton noticed that elements combine in fixed proportions (Proust's law of definite proportions, 1799) and that when they form multiple compounds, the mass ratios are simple whole numbers.

For carbon and oxygen: in CO, 12 g C combines with 16 g O. In CO2, 12 g C combines with 32 g O. Ratio 16:32 = 1:2. Only discrete units (atoms) combining in integer numbers can produce such patterns.

Dalton was colour-blind — he wrote the first scientific description of the condition (now called Daltonism) and never knew sodium emits yellow light because he couldn't see yellow. He died in 1844 and his coffin was followed by 40,000 mourners in Manchester.
items.why: Foundational scientific theories often come from outsiders working without elite credentials. Dalton was a schoolmaster, not a professor.
